new_statements.quote: [p.80 §16] As a matter of fact the actual sound is not always a, and even in the early period it is probable that in syllables preceding the final one the inherent sound was really a short neutral vowel (something like the a in abide). [p.71 fn.1] Probably pronounced Rəmán, i.e., with a short neutral vowel in the first syllable and the accent on the final syllable (as usual in Môn words). See J. Burma Research S., 1914, pp. 59, 60; 1915, p. 27.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (189 pp., sealang open download). I re-rendered djvu p.80 (= printed p.71) and djvu p.89 (= printed p.80) with ddjvu at 150 dpi and read the page images directly (not just the saved scanned). Both passages are there verbatim: p.71 footnote 1 'Probably pronounced Rəmán, i.e. with a short neutral vowel in the first syllable and the accent on the final syllable (as usual in Môn words). See J. Burma Research S., 1914, pp. 59, 60; 1915, p. 27.' and p.80 sect.16 'As a matter of fact the actual sound is not always a, and even in the early period it is probable that in syllables preceding the final one the inherent sound was really a short neutral vowel (something like the a in abide).'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Old Mon words are monosyllables or a main syllable preceded by one (rarely two) presyllables; the accent falls on the final (main) syllable, and the vowel of any preceding syllable was a short neutral (schwa-like) vowel already in the early (Old Mon) inscriptions, its spelling (a ~ i ~ u) being non-distinctive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in Blagden. (Shorto 1971: 184f., as quoted by Jenny 2005: 137, speaks of '(secondary) stress in final position' for the clause-final particle da < das, i.e. phrase-level prominence, not word-internal secondary stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Indic (Sanskrit/Pali) loans keep polysyllabic learned shapes in spelling; Blagden notes only that the inherent vowel is 'not always a'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, inferred from orthography of a dead epigraphic language (Pagan-period 'early Môn', 11th-12th c.) plus the author's knowledge of medieval and modern Mon ('as usual in Môn words'); the footnote's example Rmañ is a medieval-Mon form. Modern descriptions of spoken Mon (Jenny 2019: 282; Huffman 1990: 39) and Shorto's OM analysis relayed by Bauer 1990: 159, 164 agree: unstressed presyllable + stressed main syllable, phrase-final prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Blagden's 'early Môn' is the Old Mon of the 11th-12th c. Pagan/Prome inscriptions in Burma (Shwezigon, Myazedi etc.), i.e. classical Old Mon, not specifically the 6th-10th c. Dvaravati Old Mon of Thailand that Glottolog's oldm1242 coordinates point to; ISO omx / oldm1242 covers both stages. His footnote remark 'as usual in Môn words' generalises over Mon of all periods (he also knew modern Mon, monn1252). Any stress statement for Old Mon is necessarily inferential (dead epigraphic language): it rests on orthographic vowel neutralisation in presyllables plus the iambic pattern of modern Mon and Nyah Kur.

sources.note: p.80 sect.16: in early Mon, syllables preceding the final one probably had a short neutral vowel (like a in 'abide'); p.71 fn.1: Rman 'probably pronounced with a short neutral vowel in the first syllable and the accent on the final syllable (as usual in Môn words)'. I.e. final (main) syllable carries the accent, presyllables reduced.

sources.note: Modern spoken Mon (monn1252), not Old Mon: sect. 1.2 p.282 'Phrasal stress increases towards the end of a phrase, peaking with the last lexical word'; sect. 1.3 minor syllable = single C + ə, no register contrast.

sources.note: Sect. 1.5.1 (pp. 23-25) summarises OM phonology after Shorto 1971/Diffloth 1984 (initials, finals, vowels, epenthetic ə in clusters, 'weak presyllables') but gives no OM word-stress rule; p.137 quotes Shorto 1971: 184f. sources.citation: Bauer, Christian. 1990 [1987-88]. Numismatics, dialectology, and the periodization of Old Mon. Mon-Khmer Studies 16-17: 155-176.
sources.note: No stress rule of its own. p.159 quotes Shorto 1971: xix: 'In minor syllables we find an alternance i, u, a... there are no grounds for assuming a phonologically significant vowel distinction in this position in Old Mon'; p.164: Shorto interprets written a in man/min/mun as 'a weakened vowel in unstressed environments /ə/'.

sources.citation: Huffman, Franklin E. 1990. Burmese Mon, Thai Mon, and Nyah Kur: a synchronic comparison. Mon-Khmer Studies 16-17: 31-84.
sources.note: Modern Burmese Mon only (p.39 sect. 1.1.3): words = a single stressed syllable optionally preceded by an unstressed presyllable /Ca-/. Nothing on Old Mon.
